passage_locator.label: Chapter XX. The Way, verses 273-276
passage_locator.translation: F. Max Muller, Project Gutenberg eBook

canonical_text.quote: The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words; the best of virtues passionlessness; the best of men he who has eyes to see. This is the way, there is no other that leads to the purifying of intelligence. Go on this way! Everything else is the deceit of Mara (the tempter). If you go on this way, you will make an end of pain! The way was preached by me, when I had understood the removal of the thorns (in the flesh). You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers. The thoughtful who enter the way are freed from the bondage of Mara.

The passage says each person must make an effort, while the Tathagatas are only preachers.
The passage says the thoughtful who enter the way are freed from the bondage of Mara.

canonical_text.quote: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage. All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with a pure thought, happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him.

canonical_text.summary: Oisin tells Patrick that Niamh took him west over the sea to the Country of the Young, where he remained young and time seemed short, but on returning to Ireland he dismounted and became an aged man.

literal_observations.text: Oisin is said to have returned to Ireland long after Niamh brought him away, although the time seemed short to him.
Oisin and Niamh turn westward over the sea, which opens before them and closes behind them in waves.
During the journey they see cities, courts, white houses, palaces, a deer, a white red-eared hound, and mounted figures travelling over the waves.
Oisin names the destination the Country of the Young and the Country of Victory.
The country is described as blossoming, full of smooth plains, a grand dun, sunny houses, shining stone palaces, armed men, young women, and royal figures.
The king tells Oisin that his life there will be long lasting and that Oisin will be young forever.
Niamh warns Oisin that if he gets off the white horse in Ireland he will never return and will become old, blind, and withered.
After Oisin dismounts beside a remembered stone trough, the years come on him and the white horse leaves.

canonical_text.summary: The Tuatha de Danaan come to Ireland in mist and through the air from four northern cities, bringing four named treasures and naming leading divine or semi-divine figures among them.

literal_observations.text: The Tuatha de Danaan are called the people of the gods of Dana and are said to come through mist, air, and high air to Ireland.
Their place of origin has four cities named Falias, Gorias, Finias, and Murias.
Four wise men teach young men skill, knowledge, and perfect wisdom in those cities.
They bring four treasures from the cities: the Stone of Destiny, a sword, a Spear of Victory, and a cauldron that leaves no company unsatisfied.
Nuada is named as king of the Tuatha de Danaan, while Manannan son of Lir is said to be greater again.
Dana is named the Mother of the Gods after a list of leading women of the Tuatha de Danaan.

passage_locator.label: The Apparition of the Great Queen to Cuchulain; literal translation
passage_locator.translation: Arthur Herbert Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland
passage_locator.notes: Line numbers refer to the repository markdown source.

canonical_text.summary: Cuchulain follows a terrifying cry to Ath da Ferta, confronts a red woman driving a cow in an uncanny chariot, forces her to reveal herself as the Morrigan, hears that she guards his death and that the cow's breeding will lead to the Tain bo Cualnge, and receives her threats of future attack in eel, wolf, and heifer forms.

literal_observations.text: Cuchulain wakes in fear at a dire cry from the north, arms himself, and follows its track with Laeg.
At Ath da Ferta, Cuchulain and Laeg see an uncanny chariot with a one-footed horse, a red woman, a great man, and a cow driven before them.
Cuchulain says that the cows of Ulster are his proper care, but the woman answers for the man and gives strange names instead of plain identities.
Cuchulain springs into the woman's chariot, presses his feet on her shoulders, and demands her true name at spear-point.
The whole chariot company vanishes, and the woman appears again as a black bird on a branch.
The woman says she guards Cuchulain's death, brought the cow from the fairy-mound of Cruachan to breed by the Black Bull of Cualnge, and that this will lead to the Tain bo Cualnge.
The Morrigan threatens to attack Cuchulain in future combat as an eel, a grey wolf, and a white red-eared heifer followed by a herd.
Cuchulain answers each threatened shape with a vow of counter-injury, and the Morrigan returns to Cruachan while he goes back to Dun Imrid.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Cuchulain wakes in fear at a dire cry from the north, receives his arms from his wife, meets Laeg, and follows the sound toward Ath da Ferta.
At Ath da Ferta Cuchulain and Laeg see a chariot with a one-footed horse, a red woman, a great man with hazel staff, and a cow driven in front.
The woman answers Cuchulain's challenge with strange names; he leaps into her chariot at spear-point, demands her true name, and the whole company vanishes.

The woman reappears as a black bird, claims that she guards Cuchulain's death, and says that the cow she brought from the fairy-mound of Cruachan to breed by the Black Bull of Cualnge will lead to the Tain bo Cualnge.
The Morrigan says she will attack in eel, wolf, and white red-eared heifer forms during Cuchulain's future equal combat, and he vows to injure each form in reply.
Cuchulain returns to Dun Imrid, the Morrigan goes with her cow to the fairy-mound of Cruachan, and the tale is marked as a prelude to the Tain bo Cualnge.

canonical_text.summary: Etain is transformed by jealous sorcery into a butterfly, carried for years by a magical wind, sheltered by Angus Mac O'c, driven away again, swallowed in a cup of milk, and born anew as Etain daughter of Etar.

literal_observations.text: Fuamnach seeks out Bressal Etarlam the druid and, through sorcery, Etain is changed into a butterfly.
A great wind raised by Fuamnach's spells bears Etain away from Mider's house for seven years until she reaches Angus Mac O'c.
Angus recognizes Etain in her transformed state and keeps her in a clear-windowed bower filled with fragrant herbs.
Fuamnach later blows Etain out of the bower and the same force drives her through Ireland again in weakness and woe.
Etain falls through a roof into a golden cup of milk near Etar's wife and is swallowed with the drink.
Etain is carried in the woman's womb, born again as an earthly maiden, and said to be reborn after one thousand and twelve years.

passage_locator.label: Pillow-talk, wealth comparison, Brown Bull embassy, and Medb's resolve
passage_locator.translation: Joseph Dunn, The Ancient Irish Epic Tale Tain Bo Cualnge
passage_locator.notes: Line numbers refer to the repository markdown source.

canonical_text.summary: Medb and Ailill compare their standing and possessions at Cruachan; when their wealth proves equal except for Ailill's possession of Finnbennach, Medb seeks the Brown Bull of Cualnge from Dare, but the embassy fails after drunken boasting and she resolves to take the bull by force.

literal_observations.text: Medb rejects Ailill's claim of superiority and recounts her royal birth, military following, and prior wealth and power.
Medb says she demanded a husband without avarice, jealousy, or fear and still claims superior fortune within the marriage.
Ailill answers with his own royal standing and denies that Medb has greater riches than he does.
The couple's vessels, adornments, garments, sheep, horses, swine, and cattle are counted and mostly found equal.
Finnbennach, once a calf of Medb's cow, now belongs with Ailill's cattle, and Medb has no bull equal to him.
Medb sends macRoth to request the Brown Bull of Cualnge from Dare on rich loan terms and with further rewards.
Dare first agrees to the arrangement, but drunken messengers say the bull would be taken by force if not given willingly.
After the steward reports the boast, Dare refuses the loan, and Medb answers that the Brown Bull will be taken despite refusal.

figures.description: Queen of Connacht who asserts her own wealth and initiates the attempt to acquire the Brown Bull of Cualnge.

Ritual and mourning are judged by inward simplicity and heartfelt sorrow rather than display.
The gentleman remains courteous even in rivalry and is marked by charity, duty, and a stable path of virtue.
A son may remonstrate gently with parents, continue respectfully if ignored, and keep their age in mind with both joy and alarm.

canonical_text.summary: The Master teaches that rule should rest on honesty, charity, and example rather than punishment, that public trust outweighs even food and soldiers, and that exact language is necessary because political order fails when words no longer fit realities.

Political order depends on each relation performing its proper role: sovereign, subject, father, and son.

Confucius says political reform must begin by defining terms exactly, because disorder in language produces disorder in public action.

canonical_text.quote:
Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tzu, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes a butterfly.

canonical_text.quote:
The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao.  The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.

(Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things.

Always without desire we must be found,
If its deep mystery we would sound;
But if desire always within us be,
Its outer fringe is all that we shall see.

Under these two aspects, it is really the same; but as development takes place, it receives the different names.  Together we call them the Mystery.  Where the Mystery is the deepest is the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.

Under the aspect of having a name, the Tao is called the Mother of all things.
The passage associates absence of desire with sounding the deep mystery.

The notes explain “Rig” is almost certainly based on the Old Irish word for king (ri/rig).

Hanuman climbs a tree and chooses a hidden vantage because he expects the sorrowing queen to come into the cool retreat.
Sita appears pallid, thin from tears and fasting, in neglected dress, watched closely by fiends and giantesses.
Hanuman identifies the woman he sees as the same captive Ravana once carried through the sky and declares that she is Rama's worthy wife.
Hanuman laments that Sita, though captive and desolate, bravely endures grief and recalls Rama's past feats performed for her sake.
Hanuman recalls Sita's furrow-born origin, her choice to follow Rama into forest exile, and her present inability to notice either guards or blossoms because her thoughts remain fixed on Rama.

passage_locator.label: Book I, Canto XLIV: The Descent Of Gangá
passage_locator.translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, Project Gutenberg eBook of the Ramayana of Valmiki
passage_locator.notes: Line numbers refer to the repository markdown source for the canto narrating Bhagiratha's austerities, Gangá's descent, Jahnu's intervention, and the liberation of Sagar's sons.

canonical_text.summary: Bhagiratha continues severe penance until Śiva agrees to bear Gangá's fall. The proud river crashes onto Śiva's head and is trapped in his tangled hair until released in divided streams. Following Bhagiratha, she sanctifies beings, is swallowed and reissued by Jahnu, descends to the underworld, and frees the sons of Sagar when Bhagiratha pours the funeral libation over their dust.

literal_observations.text: Bhagiratha performs another year of extreme austerity with arms raised, one toe on the earth, and air as his food.
Śiva says he is pleased and will receive Gangá's descending waters on his head.
Gangá descends in wrath intending to sweep Śiva away, but he holds her in the tangles of his hair until her pride is checked.
Śiva finally releases the river, and seven streams emerge, with the seventh following Bhagiratha.
The river sanctifies those who touch it, and beings from many orders gather to witness or follow its course.
Jahnu angrily drinks up the river when it floods his sacrificial ground, then releases her from his ears after the gods and sages plead with him.
Bhagiratha leads Gangá to the dust of Sagar's sons, pours the funeral libation, and their spirits gain beatitude.
Brahmá praises Bhagiratha's success, names the river Bhágirathí and Tripathagá, and tells him to complete the rites for his kin.

figures.description: Royal ascetic whose prolonged penance brings Gangá to earth and to the ashes of his ancestors.

Sage whose sacrificial ground is flooded and who swallows and then reissues the river.
Creator god who appears after the ancestors are freed, praises Bhagiratha, and confirms the river's names and effect.
Bhagiratha's kinsmen whose dust receives the river and whose spirits rise in heavenly bodies.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Bhagiratha remains for a year in severe austerity, arms raised, pressing the earth with one toe and taking only air as food.
Śiva tells Bhagiratha he is pleased and will fling the mountain-born river's waves upon his head.
Gangá hears the command, descends furiously, and intends to sweep Śiva away, but he catches and confines her in the tangles of his hair.
After Bhagiratha resumes penance, Śiva ends the river's long wandering and sends her down into Vindu's lake.
Seven rivers emerge from Gangá, six flowing east and west while the seventh follows Bhagiratha after first descending on Śiva's head.
Gods, nymphs, sages, spirits, and others gather to watch the river, and those touched by the sanctified flood are freed from sin and return to the skies.
Bhagiratha rides ahead while Gangá follows him, and hosts of divine and nonhuman beings follow the stream.
Jahnu's sacrifice is flooded, he drinks up the stream in anger, and after prayer from gods and sages he releases it from his ears so that Gangá is called Jáhnavi.
Bhagiratha leads Gangá through the sea and nether caves to the dust of Sagar's sons, pours the funeral libation, and their spirits gain beatitude and rise to heaven.
Brahmá praises Bhagiratha, says the sons of Sagar have joined the blest, names the river Bhágirathí and Tripathagá, and instructs the king to complete his vow and libations.

passage_locator.label: Book VI, Cantos XXI-XXII: Ocean Threatened
passage_locator.translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, Project Gutenberg eBook
passage_locator.notes: Line numbers refer to the repository markdown source for Griffith's English verse translation of the Yuddha Kanda passage in which Rama compels Ocean's appearance and the sea bridge is begun.

canonical_text.summary: Rama prays and waits by the sea on sacred grass, vows to destroy Ocean after receiving no answer, terrifies the deep with fiery arrows and a Brahma weapon, receives Ocean's law-bound appearance and counsel, redirects the weapon northward, and then has Nala lead the vanaras in building the bridge to Lanka.

literal_observations.text: Rama reverently faces the southern ocean, lies on sacred grass, and vows that his host will cross or Ocean will perish.
After three unanswered days Rama declares that gentleness fails with the base and resolves to dry the sea with arrows.
Rama's fiery shafts strike the waters, frightening waves, sea monsters, serpents, and beings in the depths.
Lakshmana restrains Rama's arm with gentle reasoning, and voices from the air call on Rama to spare the sea.
When Rama prepares the Brahma weapon, darkness, meteors, lightning, wind, and shaking mountains make the whole cosmos register the threat.
Ocean rises in person with jewel-bright form and river retinue, says he cannot cease to be unfordable, yet promises support for a road across the waters.
At Ocean's request Rama redirects the unfailing shaft northward, where it wounds the land, creates the well of Vrana, dries waters, and is followed by a fertility boon.
Ocean names Nala as the divinely skilled builder, and the vanaras fell trees and stones to complete a massive bridge in five days and cross toward Lanka.

figures.description: Raghu's son who shifts from reverent petitioner to wrathful sea-threatener and finally to commander of the bridge crossing.
Rama's brother who briefly checks the escalation and counsels self-command.
Personified lord of the sea who appears with tributary waters, explains the law binding his nature, and offers a practical solution.
Vanara engineer identified as the son of Visvakarma and entrusted with building the bridge.
Collective labor force that uproots trees, moves stone and hills, and traverses the finished causeway.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Rama reverently faces the southern sea, lies on sacred grass, vows that the host will cross or Ocean will perish, and waits three days without reply.

Rama's fiery arrows crash into the waters, terrifying waves, sea monsters, serpents, and beings below until Lakshmana restrains him and voices from the air cry out for sparing.
Rama prepares the unfailing Brahma weapon, and darkness, thunder, meteors, lightning, violent wind, and shaking mountains register cosmic alarm.
Ocean rises in majestic jeweled form with Ganga, Sindhu, and other waters attending him, says he must remain unfordable by nature, and promises support for a road across the tide.

The vanaras uproot trees and move great stones, complete the hundred-league bridge in five days, and cross over it toward Lanka.

passage_locator.label: Book II, Cantos CXII-CXIV: The Sandals; Bharat's Return; Bharat's Departure
passage_locator.translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, Project Gutenberg eBook of the Ramayana of Valmiki
passage_locator.notes: Line numbers refer to the repository markdown source for Bharat's final plea to Ráma, the transfer of the sandals, and Bharat's return to a grieving Ayodhyá.

canonical_text.summary: After sages affirm Ráma's righteousness, Bharat begs him to return and rule, but Ráma refuses to violate their father's word. Bharat asks instead for Ráma's sandals, treats them as the delegated seat of rule, vows to live austerely outside the realm until the exile ends, and returns with them to Ayodhyá, which appears dark and joyless in Ráma's absence.

literal_observations.text: The sages praise the brothers and counsel Bharat to accept Ráma's righteous position.
Bharat asks Ráma to take up kingship because he does not believe he can protect or hold the realm as Ráma can.
Ráma embraces Bharat but insists that he will keep his father's word even if cosmic order changes.
Bharat asks Ráma to place his feet in a gold-decked pair of sandals so that the realm may be protected by them.
Bharat vows to wear hermit's dress, live on roots and fruit outside the kingdom, delegate rule to the sandals, and die in fire if Ráma does not return at the end of fourteen years.
Bharat carries the sandals on his head, receives Bharadvája's approval, and bears them toward Ayodhyá as guardians of the land.
When Bharat reaches Ayodhyá he laments that the city is mute, dark, and stripped of festivity because all grieve for banished Ráma.

When Mary brings the child to her people, they accuse her and question how they can speak with an infant in the cradle.
The child answers by identifying himself as the servant of God who has received the gospel and prophetic appointment.
The passage closes by naming the infant as Jesus, the son of Mary.

passage_locator.label: The Story of the Fisherman: sealed jar, murderous genius, and return to the vessel
passage_locator.translation: Andrew Lang, The Arabian Nights Entertainments
passage_locator.notes: Covers the fisherman's failed casts, the opening of the sealed vessel, the genius's threat, and the trick that forces the spirit back into confinement.

canonical_text.summary: An impoverished fisherman hauls up a lead-sealed jar from the sea, releases a rebel genius who vows to kill his liberator, and survives by challenging the spirit to prove it ever fit inside the vessel, then sealing it back in.

literal_observations.text: The fisherman is introduced as old and poor, supporting a wife and three children, and limiting himself to four casts a day.
His first three casts produce only an ass carcass, a rubbish-filled basket, and then stones, shells, and mud.
On the fourth cast he draws up a yellow pot sealed with lead and marked by an impressed seal.
When the fisherman opens the vessel, smoke pours out, fills sea and shore, and gathers into a giant genius.
The genius tells the fisherman that freeing him will not save him, because he has resolved to kill his deliverer.
The genius explains that he rebelled against the king of the genii, was sealed in the vessel and cast into the sea, and after centuries of captivity changed promises of reward into a vow of murder.
The fisherman pretends disbelief that so large a being could ever have fit inside the jar.
To prove the claim, the genius becomes smoke again and re-enters the vessel.
The fisherman reseals the jar, threatens to cast it back into the sea, and refuses the genius's later promise of repayment.

Rebellious supernatural being released from the sealed vessel who turns on his liberator.

comparison_claims.limitations: The comparison tracks narrative strategy, not a fixed one-to-one motif lineage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The old poor fisherman, supporting a wife and three children, makes his first cast and hauls up only the carcass of an ass.
His second and third casts fail, and the fourth brings up a heavy yellow pot instead of a fish.
The pot is sealed with lead; when opened, it releases smoke that rises, spreads over sea and shore, and condenses into a giant genius.
The genius first addresses the king of the genii, then tells the fisherman he will kill him and allow only the choice of death's manner.
The genius says that royal punishment sealed him in the vessel, that centuries passed without rescue, and that anger finally turned promised rewards into a vow to kill his liberator.
The fisherman devises a plot and claims he cannot believe so huge a being ever fit inside the vase.
The genius turns again to smoke and goes back into the vase until a voice calls out from inside.
The fisherman shuts the lead cover on the vase and threatens to cast it into the sea again and warn future fishermen.
Unable to escape because of the enchantment, the genius tries cunning and promises repayment, but the fisherman refuses and introduces another cautionary story.

passage_locator.label: The Arabian Nights: Scheherazade volunteers and secures the dawn reprieve
passage_locator.translation: Andrew Lang, The Arabian Nights Entertainments
passage_locator.notes: Primary focus falls on lines 244-348 and 410-435; lines 351-409 begin the embedded Merchant and Genius tale that activates the reprieve.

canonical_text.summary: Scheherazade persuades her father to give her to Schahriar, arranges for Dinarzade to request a story before dawn, and wins repeated postponement of execution by leaving each tale unfinished at daybreak.

literal_observations.text: Scheherazade is introduced as the elder daughter of the grand-vizir and is described as learned, beautiful, clever, and courageous.
She says she is resolved to stop the Sultan's bride-killing practice and save the girls and mothers of the city.
Scheherazade asks her father to let her be the bride, while the grand-vizir protests that the command would force him to kill his own daughter.
The Sultan accepts the plan but warns the grand-vizir that he must carry out Scheherazade's execution himself or lose his own head.
Scheherazade instructs Dinarzade to wake her before dawn and ask for one of her stories so the people may be delivered from terror.
On the wedding night Scheherazade obtains permission for Dinarzade to sleep in the chamber and waits for the planned request.
Dinarzade asks for a story before sunrise, the Sultan permits it, and Scheherazade begins the tale.
At daybreak Scheherazade stops speaking and implies that the rest of the tale will be more wonderful if she is allowed to live another day.
Schahriar postpones her death to hear the end, and the same pattern recurs on the following mornings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Scheherazade is introduced as the grand-vizir's elder daughter and is praised for learning, beauty, courage, and intelligence.
Scheherazade declares that she means to stop the Sultan's practice and deliver girls and mothers from the fate hanging over them.
She asks to be the Sultan's bride, and the grand-vizir refuses because obedience would require him to kill her himself.
Schahriar warns the grand-vizir that he must take Scheherazade's life himself or lose his own head.

passage_locator.label: The Second Book, Hero Twins in Xibalba
passage_locator.start: It was not long, however, until Hun-Came and Vukub-Came
passage_locator.notes: Public-domain Project Gutenberg text of Spence's 1908 English edition.

canonical_text.summary: Hun-Ahpu and Xbalanque are lured toward Xibalba, avoid traps that defeated their fathers, pass underworld houses and ballgame challenges, suffer a beheading episode, die together by design, return in transformed disguise, and defeat the princes of Xibalba by refusing to revive them.

literal_observations.text: Hun-Came and Vukub-Came hear the twins playing ball and decide to lure them to the Underworld.
The twins plant canes at home so their family can read their welfare from whether the canes remain green or wither.
The twins cross the river of blood and river Papuhya, expose wooden decoys, avoid a red-hot stone, and pass the House of Gloom.
The twins survive the House of Lances through ants and bribed lancers, then survive houses of cold, tigers, and fire.
In the House of Bats, Hun-Ahpu is beheaded by Camazotz, yet the brothers later emerge uninjured from the ordeals.
The brothers die together on a funeral pile, their powdered bones enter the river, and they reappear in changed forms before defeating the Xibalban princes.

canonical_text.summary: In primeval darkness Hurakan calls earth into being, the gods take counsel, and wooden mannikins are created as a failed human attempt. By Hurakan's will, floodwaters rise and drown the wooden mannikins while resin falls from heaven.
Birds dismember the wooden people, and household animals and tools accuse and attack them.
Houses, trees, and caverns refuse refuge, and the ruined race is said to survive as monkeys.

canonical_text.quote: Some one, O Gish, who like thee / In the field was born and / Whom the mountain has reared

literal_observations.text: Gish tells his mother that a heavenly object fell upon him in a dream and became too heavy for him to endure.
The mother of Gish says the dream points to someone like Gish, born in the field and reared by the mountain.

passage_locator.label: Birth of Rustem; Simurgh aid, prodigious growth, and the white elephant feat

canonical_text.summary: During Rudabeh's dangerous labor, Zal burns the Simurgh's feather and the bird appears to guide the birth of Rustem. The white elephant at Sistan breaks loose by night and tramples people to death.
Rustem forces his way out, confronts the elephant alone, bends his iron mace with the blow, and kills the beast in one strike.

The Simurgh gives Zal a feather to burn in danger and then carries him back to his father.
